newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia's highest paid chief executive resigns.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia's highest paid chief executive resigns.

text.p: Australia's largest retailer Coles Myer Ltd on Monday announced the surprise resignation of managing director Peter Bartels, the highest paid chief executive in the country.

The company, which has faced lower profits and investor dissatisfaction in the four years since Bartels was poached from the top role at major Australian brewer Foster's, said Bartels' departure would bring stability.

In a statement delivered after the local market's close, Coles said it faced the unacceptable timetable next July of having to grapple with both the retirement of chairman Nobby Clark and the end of Bartels' contract as chief executive.
"Both Peter and the company agreed that this was not desirable and that it was in the best interest of the company to stagger the changes and achieve greater continuity," Clark said.
Bartels will be replaced by Dennis Eck, Coles Myer's chief operating officer of the company's business units division.
Eck, 53, left his position as president of U.S. supermarket chain Vons Cos Inc to join Coles in 1994 as a consultant.

He was appointed managing director of the profitable supermarkets division in May 1994, group managing director of the "basic needs" unit in November 1995 and to the business units division in April this year.

He is left with the task of rebuilding department store margins and restoring profit growth to the overall group, which in October unveiled a 34 percent plunge in annual net profit to A$280.4 million ($224 million) for the year to July 28, its lowest bottom line in eight years.
Analysts said Eck's retailing pedigree appeared solid but they said the new chief executive's department store skills were unproven.

"I think the biggest query on Eck is that...he clearly has supermarket expertise, but hasn't had expertise in department store retailing and that's where his two big jobs lie, K-mart and Myer," said Prudential-Bache Securities analyst John Burgess, referring to two of the company's key retail divisions.
Analysts were divided over the fairness of Bartels' departure but most saw it as the final move in installing a fresh board to confront Coles' remaining operational problems.

"There a lot of new people now heading up the major divisions of Coles so I think Eck's got a good fresh team...therefore management is arguably in a better position than it has even been to bring out the benefits," Burgess said.
The analysts said Bartels' exit mostly had been priced into the company's shares which closed three cents higher at A$4.52.
"I think the market had basically been factoring this in...and you might see 10 cents (added to) the share price but I don't think it will last," a Sydney-based analyst said.

Bartels had been under pressure through 1996 due to the group's financial performance. The disclosure of his A$2.8 million 1995/96 pay package further enraged Coles shareholders at the company's annual meeting last month.
The revelation sparked calls from Prime Minister John Howard and Treasurer Peter Costello for executive wage restraint.
Bartels was also regarded in the investment community as being close to Coles director and former chairman Solomon Lew who was embroiled in a funding/share buying controversy over the past two years.

Lew was forced to stand down as chairman due to the so-called Yannon dispute which involved funding of Coles share purchases by Lew through a complicated financial scheme which cost Coles A$18 million.
